title: What the Name Outlived
aliases: Sixteen Hundred Pillars and No Palace
logline: Two monuments about nine hundred metres apart in one ancient sacred city, walked between in a single morning: at the first, every part of a famous building is still standing in order and the building is gone; at the second, the building is still standing and has lost half its height. Neither name moved by a letter.
human_question: One name can survive losing the whole of the thing it names, and another can survive losing half of it. So what was a name ever attached to?

place.what_kind_of_place: Two monuments in the same ruined capital, a walk of ten or fifteen minutes apart, and the ground between them. The first is a field of stone pillars on bare red earth, set on a low brick-faced terrace in the busiest precinct of the old city: about sixteen hundred of them, forty rows of forty, most standing about twelve feet clear of the ground, rough grey granite blotched with lichen and uneven at the top where the beams were taken away. They are the ground-floor colonnade of a building the chronicle describes as nine storeys high with a roof of metal plates, and the colonnade is all that is left of it; a small modern chapter house stands in the middle of the grid, on the old pillars, timber-sided under a pale tiled roof, and it is in use. The second is a colossal dome of bare baked brick standing above the treeline of the same plain, unplastered and unwhitewashed, so the courses run visibly across the curve, on a paved terrace inside a much larger monastic precinct that is now mostly foundations and grass. Conservation has been running on it for decades: scaffolding on the upper works, stacks of newly fired brick in the shade, lime mortar, masons setting courses into patched sections of the skin. Between the two is the ordinary ground of a working sacred city — a path, low masonry, shade trees, a green iron railing, a power line across the sky, and people walking the circuit all day. Both monuments are living places of worship and neither is a ruin anyone has finished with.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: This is the group's most architectural film and it is carried by hard geometry and by two vertical moves. First the grid: from anywhere inside the pillar field the rows line up, break and line up again as the camera moves, so a complete floor plan keeps assembling and dissolving without anyone touching it, and from directly above it resolves into one ruled rectangle drawn on the ground in stone. Second the walk: a continuous traverse out of that rectangle, across open ground, with a brown dome rising over the canopy ahead until it fills the sky. Third the curve read from underneath: standing on the paving at the base, the mass goes up out of the frame in visible courses, and the four projecting frontispieces that read as buildings from a distance turn out to be knee-high to the thing they are attached to. The two verticals are the film. One looks up and finds nothing where eight more storeys should be. The other looks up and keeps finding brick, and still stops short of where the thing used to stop.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Nothing here is under the crew's control, and the only continuous thing is the walk. At the pillar field the shadow of sixteen hundred uprights turns across the earth all day like a sundial with no dial; the terrace is too hot for bare feet at midday and empties, and fills again in the evening. On the traverse the plain is open and weather crosses it in full view for half an hour before it arrives. At the stupa the scaffold is up one month and down another, a patch of new brick is a different colour from the old until it weathers, and the stone paving goes from cold to unwalkable and back. On full-moon days both precincts fill. The formal proceedings inside the small chapter house in the middle of the grid are not a public event and are not a thing that happens for anybody to watch.
place.when_it_looks_best: The middle of a clear day, counter-intuitively, is when this particular film is strongest: the shadows shorten to nothing, the pillar field reads purely as a plan, and the dome reads as mass and course rather than as a silhouette. The first hour gives the avenues and the walk; the traverse wants a morning, because the second monument stands to the north-east of the first and is best approached with the sun behind or beside the camera rather than in it. The dry months of roughly May to September give hard light and open sky. After the north-east rains, roughly December to February, the earth is dark, the lichen is bright, the brick is deeper and the plain is green, which is a different and equally good film. Full-moon days are the busiest and the hardest days on which to film anyone honestly, so they are a decision and not a default.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A walk between two enormous things in one morning, with a clean shape and a real story at each end. Dawn down one avenue of forty stones; the grid assembling and breaking as the camera walks it; one pillar at arm's length with its tool marks and broken top; the whole rectangle from above and the empty sky above that; then out through the gate, along the path, past low foundations, with a brown hill of brick coming up over the trees; sandals left in rows; the scale arriving all at once at the base; the courses running away up the curve until the eye cannot separate them; and the last frame looking straight up at a mass that stops short of where it used to stop. Someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete piece with a beginning, a journey and a payoff.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration rather than an argument, and the demonstration is run twice in opposite directions. The voice never contradicts anything on screen. At the first monument it points at a famous name that refers to a nine-storey building with a metal roof, and underneath the name a complete set of parts in perfect order with the thing itself missing — the old books' own division test, already carried out by fire and invasion and eight hundred years. At the second it points at one name in use for an estimated ninety-three million separate fired objects, none of which is the thing the name refers to, over a mass that has lost roughly half its height without the name altering by a letter. Separately each place says a name is not the thing. Walked in one morning they say something neither could: that the name does not mind which way its object fails. It does not need the whole, and it does not need the size.

sequence.on_screen: First light, ground level, camera low and square on to one avenue: forty pillars in a single receding line on bare red earth, mist still in the big trees at the edge of the field, the tops of the stones uneven against a pale sky.
sequence.voice: A chronicle written in Pali describes what stood here. Nine storeys. A hundred cubits on each side and a hundred cubits high. A thousand chambers, and a hundred window-chambers to every floor. A roof of copper plates, which is where the name everybody still uses comes from. Nobody alive has seen it.

sequence.on_screen: The camera walks slowly sideways across the front of the field. The rows come into alignment, collapse into a thicket, and come back into alignment again, over and over, as the angle changes.
sequence.voice: The old books have a category for a thing like this. They call it a collective concept, and they define it very plainly: what the mind takes to be there because a number of separate materials have been gathered and connected to each other in some particular way. The examples they use are a table, a chair, a bed, a chariot.

sequence.on_screen: One pillar at arm's length, filling the frame: grey granite, lichen in yellow and black, a chisel-cut notch near the top where a beam was seated, the crown broken and weathered round. Then a slow pull back until it is one upright among hundreds.
sequence.voice: And the books give the test that settles what a thing like this is. Divide it, and see what is left. Pull cloth apart and you have thread, and there is no cloth anywhere among the threads. Here the dividing has already been done for us, by fire and by invasion and by a long time. What is left is the parts — and even these may not be the first building's. It was rebuilt again and again, and the sources do not agree which rebuilding these pillars belong to, or whose it was. The name did not move either way.

sequence.on_screen: The small modern hall standing on the old pillars at the height the first floor used to be; then the vertical. The camera lifts from between two pillars and rises straight up, the stones falling away below until forty rows of forty resolve into a single ruled rectangle on the ground, and it keeps climbing through the levels that are not there. If the drone is refused, the same beat is a held tilt from the hall's roofline into completely empty sky, long enough to be uncomfortable.
sequence.voice: That is one storey. The chronicle says there were nine. A name is what makes a thing known, and it is not the thing it makes known. It is under no obligation to shrink when the thing does, or to go away when the thing goes. This is a floor plan, complete, to the last pillar. Everything except the building.

sequence.on_screen: The traverse. Down the steps, out through the gate in the iron railing, and a continuous walk across the old city: the path, low foundations in the grass, stone posts, shade trees, the back of the crowd going the other way. Ahead, over the canopy, a brown dome comes up and keeps getting bigger.
sequence.voice: The plainest word these books have for a collection is a heap. Everything of one kind, spread out across distance, gathered by the mind into one and then given a single word. They are careful to say they mean it literally, the way you would say a great heap of water, and not the loose way you would say a great log. And they add a second thing: a heap is also a portion. What we have just walked out of was both. A heap of stone, and, by the chronicle's count, the bottom ninth of something.

sequence.on_screen: Arrival. Sandals in rows at the edge of the paving, bare feet on hot stone, and then one of the projecting frontispieces square on: dressed stone set into brick courses, a small offering table, and above it brickwork running away up the curve until the courses are too fine for the eye to separate.
sequence.voice: A king began this in the third century. Some accounts say he finished it; others say his son did. The count is an estimate, and the estimate is ninety-three million bricks. Every one of them was pressed in a mould, fired, carried and set in mortar by somebody who could hold it in one hand. Not one of them is the thing the name refers to.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff, and the answering shot to beat four. From the paving at the base, the camera tilts straight up the flank: courses, the shoulder of the dome, the square chamber, the spire, scaffold poles, and then sky. No cut, no crane, no aircraft. Hold on the sky above the spire for as long as beat four held on the sky above the pillars.
sequence.voice: Look up, the same way we looked up an hour ago. Back there, looking up found nothing: the parts, and then sky. Here it keeps finding brick, and then it stops. This stands about seventy-one metres. Finished, the estimates put it near a hundred and twenty-two, which for a while made it the third-tallest structure on earth after two pyramids. It failed, it was rebuilt smaller, it stood in jungle, and men have been putting brick back into it for forty years. Through all of that the name has not changed by one letter. One name lost the whole of what it named. The other lost half the size of what it named. Neither of them noticed.

sequence.on_screen: Dusk, from distance and staying there, on ground that holds both in one sightline if such ground exists: the field of uprights flat and dark in the foreground, the dome behind it losing its surface, a lamp or two already lit at each. Nobody approached, nobody singled out, nothing lit by the crew.
sequence.voice: The books that take things apart like this are careful about why they do it. Never to announce that nothing is there and nobody is home. Only to loosen a grip. Nothing said tonight has moved one of those stones or taken one brick out of that wall. Both names are still the words everybody here uses, and they were never the things.

concept_merge.why_together:
Two digests, and now two monuments, and the second pairing is the reason this record exists in its present form. Read fresh, C084 supplies the category, the definition and the test. The Pradeepika defines paññatti as both the thing made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25], lists the collective concept first among its eight kinds and gives for it the earth, mountains, rivers and the sea [C084-P:L29], and notes that a name-concept is a name laid either over the ultimates or over those eight kinds of concept [C084-P:L47]. The Mārgaya's gloss of the collective concept is the one the first monument needs, because its examples are made things rather than landforms: what the mind takes to be there on the strength of a number of separate materials having been gathered and connected to one another in some particular way, a table, a chair, a bed, a mat, a pillow, a chariot [C084-M:L15]. It then states the test, which is to divide a thing, because whatever disappears under division was never a single thing to begin with, there being no cloth anywhere among the threads [C084-M:L7]. C077 supplies the plainest available word for the same operation and the reason anyone would run it. Khandha means collection: everything of one kind, however divided, taken by the mind as one and called by a single name [C077-M:L10]; the Pradeepika sorts the word's several senses, keeps only the heap sense, the one used when speaking of a great heap of water, sets aside the merely conventional sense used of a great log, and says the aggregates are characterised by heap-ness and by being portions [C077-P:L36–L42], then shows a whole mass of one kind lumped together on every side and displayed under one word [C077-P:L44].

The merge itself is the argument. One name laid over an assemblage has exactly two ways of failing, and until now this group carried a separate film for each of them. At the first monument the parts survive and the whole is gone: forty rows of forty granite pillars, a complete ground plan, and the nine-storey copper-roofed building the chronicle describes is simply not there — and the building was rebuilt so many times that the sources do not agree which rebuilding the standing pillars belong to, so the name may be detached twice over. At the second the whole survives and has shrunk: an estimated 93.3 million hand-laid bricks, once about 122 metres and by the usual reckoning the third-tallest structure on earth, now about 71, with the name unaltered by a letter. Filmed apart, each place says the same single sentence, that a name is not the thing. Filmed as one walk they say what neither could alone: the name is indifferent to which way its object fails. It does not need the whole and it does not need the size. That also hands the film a structure it did not have — parts without a whole, then whole diminished, then the question of what the name was ever attached to — and it is why the two records were collapsed into one rather than left to repeat each other in the same city.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the collective concept can be tested to destruction from both ends in a single morning, on real ground, with nothing arranged. Ordinarily the point of the division test is that a whole dissolves when you divide it; at the first monument the division has already been performed by history and the result is lying on the earth, parts all present, in order, countable, and the named whole entirely absent. At the second the object is emphatically present and the test has been run on its magnitude instead: the referent lost roughly half of itself and the designation did not register the loss. Set side by side they show that the name was never tracking either the completeness or the extent of its object, which is a stronger statement than either monument makes on its own and one that no analogy could stage. C077 keeps the film honest while it says so. The reason the books count at all is to loosen the grip of 'this is me, this is mine' [C077-M:L24; C077-P:L982–L984], not to announce that nothing is there; the same compendium insists that suffering really exists and that what is missing is only a separate owner of it [C077-P:L2292–L2298]. Neither digest licenses telling anybody in either precinct that the place they have come to is merely a word.

concept_links.why:
This film is the collective concept taken to both of its limits, and the sources supply the category, the definition, the test and, for the second monument, the example itself. The Mārgaya defines samūha-paññatti as what the mind takes to be there because many separate materials have been gathered and connected to one another in a particular way, and the examples it gives are constructed objects: a table, a chair, a bed, a mat, a pillow, a chariot [C084-M:L15]; the Pradeepika places the same category first among its eight kinds of concept and illustrates it with the earth, mountains, rivers and the sea [C084-P:L29]. A colonnade of about sixteen hundred pillars is that category with the connecting taken away and the materials left standing; a dome of an estimated ninety-three million bricks is the same category built to the largest scale a hand-sized unit has ever reached, and it is the sources' own mountain example made by people. The Mārgaya's division test is the reason the first site is an argument rather than an illustration: divide a thing, and whatever disappears under division was never a single thing, since there is no cloth anywhere among the threads [C084-M:L7]. There the division is historical fact and the disappearance is complete. The definition of paññatti as both the thing made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25], with the note that a name-concept is a name laid over the ultimates or over the eight kinds of concept [C084-P:L47], is what the film can observe directly at both ends of the walk: at one the name is in daily working use and its referent is not present at all, at the other the name is in daily working use and its referent is half the size the name was given to. The Mārgaya's separation of the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it conveys, which is not — with its example of a three-syllable word in which no single sound and no combination of the sounds is the name, the name being what turns up in the person listening [C084-M:L21] — is the exact miniature of the pillar field: all the parts present, and the thing named not among them.

The digest's own limits are load-bearing at two living sacred sites and they are written into the voice rather than bolted on. The film never tells anyone that the name they use is wrong; it says the opposite, following the page that puts ground and mountain among the things that are not ultimately existent, being a modification of elements, and then records without embarrassment that people call them ground and mountain [C084-P:L55]. The existent and non-existent pairs are technical Abhidhamma categories and are never rendered as true and false. And nothing here supports 'nothing is real' or 'language constructs reality': the sources keep the ultimates fully real and treat conventional wholes as valid in their own domain, which is why the last beat ends by saying that nothing said has moved a stone or taken out a brick.

C077 supplies the plain word that carries the film across the ground between the two monuments, and it supplies the guards. Khandha is glossed simply as collection: everything of one kind, however divided as past, future and present, taken by the mind as one collection and the whole of it called by a single name [C077-M:L10]. The Pradeepika sorts the word's senses and keeps only the heap sense, the one used when one speaks of a great heap of water, explicitly setting aside the conventional sense used of a great log, and states that the aggregates are characterised by heap-ness and by being portions [C077-P:L36–L42]; it then shows a whole mass of one kind lumped together on every side and displayed under a single word [C077-P:L44]. Both halves do work here, and they do different work at each end. A ground-floor colonnade is a heap of one kind and also a portion, by the chronicle's count the bottom ninth of something, which is what the first vertical is about; a stack of newly fired replacement brick sitting in the shade beside the largest brick structure ever built is the heap sense twice over at two scales in one frame. The digest's first prohibition governs the whole film: 'you do not exist' and 'the self is an illusion' are not what the source says. The counting exists to loosen the sense of 'this is me, this is mine' that settles on each heap [C077-M:L24; C077-P:L982–L984], and the same compendium says elsewhere that suffering really exists and that only a separate owner of it is missing [C077-P:L2292–L2298]; beat 8 exists to hold that line for both precincts at once. Two further limits are written in rather than mentioned. The enumeration is not offered to the viewer as a technique: where this source hands over a practice of taking a thing to pieces it puts it inside monastic discipline, under a teacher, with preconditions [C077-P:L1493–L1497], and this film offers nobody an exercise. And the inferior-and-superior ladder in the same range belongs to a cosmology of rebirth and a pre-modern social order [C077-P:L203–L207], so no stone, no brick, no rebuild, no reign, no era and neither of the two monuments is graded against the other.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a name can go on working perfectly after the thing it names has gone, and can go on working perfectly after the thing it names has halved, and that noticing this takes nothing away from either place or from the people who come to them. The proof is on the ground twice in one morning and needs no belief: every part of a famous building present, in order, countable, and the building absent; and then an estimated ninety-three million hand-sized objects present, in place, and the thing they were piled into standing at half the height the name was given to.
what_must_be_real: Two living sacred sites in the busiest precincts of an ancient city, filmed as such. No act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repositioned or lit for filming; nothing is arranged, no offering placed, no lamp lit and no circuit walked for the camera. The formal monastic proceedings held in the building at the centre of the pillar grid are not a public event and are not filmed at all. Nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera appears: people are filmed at distance and in the ordinary course of the day, never singled out, never framed as an example of devotion or of anything else, and no child is a character. Separate, freely given consent from any conservation worker or mason filmed close, who are filmed as people doing skilled paid work on a hot day and never as an illustration of a doctrine; no brick is moved, laid, unlaid or handled for a shot. Consent from the site authority and from each resident community, which are separate permissions for two separate precincts. The walk between them is a real walk on the public route and is not cleared, staged or repeated for coverage. The crew observes each site's own rules, barefoot and covered, without exception for equipment. The other very famous monuments standing between and around the two are not the subject of this film and do not become one: a distant white spire on the skyline is the most they get. The historical material is handled as the record has it, held apart into what is certain and what is disputed: the chronicle's figures are said aloud as the chronicle's figures and the brick count, the volume and the original height are said aloud as estimates, every time. The reigns that raised either monument are not narrated as merit or greatness, the labour is not narrated as sacrifice or devotion, and the repeated destructions and the recorded monastic quarrel are recorded as layers with their provenance attached and are never adjudicated.
position_hint: middle: the group's cleanest statement of a name outliving its object, made twice and in opposite directions, and it works best after a viewer has already watched a name and a thing come apart once somewhere less severe. It is also the group's longest single movement — one continuous journey with two held vertical frames in it — which is easier to give an audience already inside the series. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Telling anyone in either precinct, in effect, that the place they have come to is 'only a name'. The C084 digest forbids telling a participant the name they use is wrong, and in the most visited parts of the sacred city that risk is not theoretical; beat 8 exists to refuse it and the whole voice is written so that the analysis lands on the name and never on the people.
Overreaching into 'nothing is real' or 'language constructs reality': the sources keep sound, colour, feeling and mind fully real, and treat conventional wholes as valid in their own domain.
'You do not exist' or 'the self is an illusion': the C077 digest rules both out, and the counting is stated there as a way of loosening a grip, not as a denial.

Treating the existent and non-existent pairs as 'true' and 'false' names. They are technical categories, and the same passage that places ground and mountain among the non-existent also records that people call them ground and mountain.

Handing the viewer the enumeration as an exercise. The source that does hand over a practice of taking a thing to pieces places it inside monastic discipline, under a teacher, with preconditions; this film offers nobody a technique.

Narrating the building of either monument as devotion, sacrifice or royal greatness, or either reign as merit. The chronicle's own statement about how the first was paid for belongs in the historical thread with its provenance attached, not in the voice as a virtue, and the record is effectively silent about how the second was built.

Adjudicating the destructions or the quarrel. The first building was burnt, cut down in storeys, deliberately pulled down for material, damaged in invasions and rebuilt at least eight times; the second stands on ground the chronicle tradition connects to a dispute with an older monastic community. Both records were written and continued by parties to them. They go in the historical thread as layers and never into the voice as anyone's grievance or anyone's due.

Stating the chronicle's dimensions as measurements. Nine storeys, a hundred cubits square, a hundred cubits high, a thousand chambers, a hundred window-chambers to each storey: these are the chronicle's figures and the voice says so. The commonly repeated modern figure of four hundred feet to a side contradicts the chronicle outright and is not used.

Stating the brick count, the original height or the volume of the second monument as established fact. They are estimates, they differ substantially between sources, and the voice says 'the estimate is' every time.

Building the payoff on low raking light making a ruin legible. That is another film in this slate and this one must not repeat it. The absorbed record's payoff was exactly that — the last twenty minutes of sun turning a brick curve to grain — and it has been deliberately replaced. The light here is texture and a clock; the payoff is the pair of verticals and the two held frames of empty sky above them.
Building the payoff on a shadow, which belongs to the group's opening film, or on a low sun making a shape legible for the first time. The geometry in this film is legible at noon and is meant to be.

Letting the traverse become a tour. The walk exists because the two arguments have to be made by the same person in the same morning; it is not an excuse for a montage of the city, and every famous thing passed on the way stays passed.

Letting the second monument swamp the first. It is very much larger and very much more photogenic, and a film that spends twelve minutes at the pillar field and forty at the dome has lost the merge. The two halves are equal and the walk is the hinge.
Letting the two famous neighbours of the first monument take the film over. They are the reason that ground is busy and they are not the subject, and a beautiful frame of either does not belong here.

Drone permission over this precinct is genuinely doubtful and may simply be refused. Civil Aviation Authority registration and permit plus Department of Archaeology clearance are both required, and a man was arrested on 17 September 2025 for flying at the great stupa a few hundred metres from the first monument without archaeological permission. The film is built so that it survives refusal: the first vertical can be made from the ground as a held tilt from the chapter house roofline into empty sky, the grid is legible along the avenues at eye level, a raised position outside the precinct gives the plan at an angle, and the second vertical — the payoff — is a tilt from the paving that needs no aircraft at all.
Aestheticising conservation labour, or letting a mason's hands stand in for an idea about devotion. They are hands doing paid skilled work.
A scaffold or a fresh patch of new brick sitting in the middle of a frame, and the matching temptation to hide the conservation work. The film shows it; it does not frame around it.
Reaching for the unconditioned. The one thing this compendium says has no heap is the one thing no shot is, and the film does not let a beautiful dark frame imply it.
Crowd and consent pressure, which is at its worst on full-moon days and on the through-routes between the great monuments, where the ability of any individual to refuse a camera is lowest.

District concentration. This film's district stands at nine films in the slate's Films per district table, against the working rule that seven closes a district, and GRP-01 alone puts three films there: this one, IDEA-0008 on the sacred hill east of the city, and IDEA-0012, whose second figure some sources place across the boundary in the neighbouring district. The merge reduced the count by one and the archetype is distinct (a colonnade and a floor plan first and a stupa second, not a hill, a riddle or a rock-cut figure), but the concentration is real, it is not resolved by this record, and it is a question for Chathura rather than a reason to move a film that the story holds here.
drop_if: Filming cannot happen without intruding on worship at either site, or on the resident community's use of the building at the centre of the grid, or without both site authorities and both communities understanding and agreeing to what the film is doing.
Access is offered only on terms that require the film to present either monument as a devotional or national achievement.
Neither the overhead rectangle nor any honest ground substitute for the first vertical can be obtained, which would leave the film with a field of stones and only half an argument.
The walk between the two cannot be made and filmed as a continuous journey on the public route, which would turn the merge back into two short films cut together.
The estimates for the second monument turn out to be unsupportable enough that the film would have to state a number it does not believe.

connections.note: This film is the merge of the two. IDEA-0011 was the same concept pair in the same ancient city on the opposite case — a mass of millions of small identical units under a name that did not change by a letter while the thing it names lost half its height — and its entire subject, research, historical thread, verified images and risks have been taken into this record, which now visits both monuments in one walk. The reason for merging rather than keeping both is stated in concept_merge: one name over an assemblage has two failure modes, this group had a film for each, and together in one traverse they show that the name is indifferent to which way its object fails. IDEA-0011 is now a different film at a different place and nothing about the stupa belongs to it any more.

Same primary concept, opposite direction, and a different city on a different coast. That film holds a cast-bronze figure on a sea cliff whose metal never changed while the name it carried as a god left it for three centuries in the ground and then came back; this one holds two names that never left while the things they name lost their whole and half their size. There the thing stays and the name comes and goes; here the name stays and the thing goes. No sea, no metal and no burial belongs in this film.

Shares the primary concept and the district, and must stay clear of it. That film is a sacred hill, a stairway and a question put to a king about a tree; this one is flat ground, hard geometry and two vertical frames. No climb, no terrace at a summit and no dialogue-riddle belongs here.

A shape with a name and a size that is not made of anything, and two names over assemblages that are unmistakably there and unmistakably incomplete. No shadow and no shape-concept payoff belongs in this film; the opening film owns both.

A rock named, by a chronicle written centuries later, after a lion whose only basis was a sculpted shape of brick and plaster, now gone but for its paws; against a name whose parts are still standing in order and whose building is not there. There the basis of the name was never a being; here the basis was a building and it is gone.

The same concept pair on a set of figures where the count is the one thing nobody disputes and every name is a proposal, against two places where the names are the one thing nobody disputes and the things they name are gone or halved.

The other film in this group built on two locations rather than one, and deliberately a different use of the pair: that one holds two statues apart and lets the stones contradict the legend that joins them, while this one walks continuously from one monument to the other and uses the journey itself as the argument's hinge.

selection.reason: Merged with IDEA-0011 at Chathura's instruction, because the merge tells the philosophical story better than either film did alone. The two were the closest pair in the group: same ancient city, same concept pair, same argument approached from two sides. One name laid over an assemblage can fail in exactly two ways, and the group had a separate film for each — parts surviving with the whole gone at the colonnade, the whole surviving at half its size at the stupa. Separately they repeat one sentence. Together, walked in a single morning, they show that the name is indifferent to which way its object fails: it needs neither the whole nor the size. That also gives the film a three-part structure it did not have, and it frees a location slot in an over-concentrated district.

review.note: This film was confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25, after he had edited it by hand. The verdict was reset to pending on 2026-09-26 because a GRP-01 audit corrected voice lines, and under standing decision 9 a changed body invalidates an older verdict. His wording was kept everywhere except the lines being fixed; the locations, the merge, the concepts and the treatment are unchanged. The changes, and why: (1) beat 3 said the standing pillars were 'raised where they stand by a king called Parakramabahu'. That attribution rests only on popular pages, the English Wikipedia article links the pillars to Dutugemunu's building instead (uncited), and nothing scholarly settles it, so the voice now says the building was rebuilt again and again and the sources do not agree which rebuilding these pillars belong to, or whose it was; the 'unanimous' claim was deleted from what_is_certain, the dispute is set out in what_is_disputed, why_here, concept_merge and how_it_binds were hedged to match, and the drop_if that depended on the attribution was removed. It also takes Parakramabahu out of this film's voice. (2) Beat 6 said the stupa was finished around 301 'after he was dead'; completion is credited to Mahasena in some accounts and to his son Kithsirimevan in others, so the voice now says only that some accounts say the king finished it and others say his son did, and it no longer names Mahasena, who is named in IDEA-0012. (3) 'The bottom fortieth of something' (beat 5 and the C077 link) was an arithmetic slip: a nine-storey building's ground floor is the bottom ninth, and it is now said as the chronicle's count. (4) Beat 4's 'There were nine' is now 'The chronicle says there were nine', because the same tradition gives nine, then seven, then five. (5) The why_here paragraph and the IDEA-0004 connection described a rock-cut void in this city that no longer exists; IDEA-0004 is now a bronze figure on a sea cliff on the east coast, so the paragraph now distinguishes this film from the group's current neighbours (the mango-riddle hill and the two standing figures) and the connection is a mirror of the bronze film; the IDEA-0003 note was also updated. (6) The evidence note no longer calls the locations Chathura's; under decision 2 they were proposed by Claude and confirmed by him. (7) The district risk now records that the film's district stands at nine films, above the seven that closes a district, with three from GRP-01. (8) The nineteenth-century swap of the two great stupas' names, already in what_is_disputed was re-verified and a source added; it stays out of the voice. Still unverified: which building the standing pillars belong to, whether they were re-erected in modern times, the stupa's brick count, height and volume (all estimates), and every permission, including drone permission, which should be assumed refused.

suggested_location.region: Anuradhapura District, North Central Province — both monuments stand inside the sacred city of the ancient capital, the colonnade in the Mahavihara precinct between the Ruwanwelisaya stupa and the Sri Maha Bodhi, and the stupa about nine hundred metres to the north-east in the Jetavana monastery precinct, east of Abhaya Wewa
suggested_location.why_here:
Because the two monuments together are the collective concept tested to destruction from both ends, and they are close enough to be walked between in one morning. The collective concept is what the mind takes to be there because many separate materials have been gathered and connected in a particular way. At the colonnade the materials are still gathered, still in order, forty rows of forty, and what they were connected into is completely absent: a name that refers to a nine-storey building with a metal roof is in daily working use over a field of ground-floor pillars, and the history may double the detachment, because the building was rebuilt many times and the sources do not agree which rebuilding the standing stones belong to: popular Sri Lankan site pages give them to the twelfth-century work of Parakramabahu I, the English Wikipedia article associates the pillars with Dutugemunu's original building without a citation, and no scholarly or excavation source settling it was found. At the stupa the opposite failure has occurred. The materials are an estimated 93.3 million baked bricks and the assemblage is emphatically there; what it has lost is roughly half its height, from something near 122 metres to about 71, and the name has not altered by a letter. That is the argument no single site in this group could make and no analogy could invent: the name does not need the whole and it does not need the size.

It also films, and it films as one continuous piece rather than two. The first monument is a very large floor plan drawn on open ground in hard grey granite, so the grid assembles and breaks continuously as the camera moves and resolves from directly above into one ruled rectangle with nothing whatever on top of it. The second is a bare brick mass whose courses are legible from the paving to the spire, read from underneath. Between them is a real walk on a public route across the old city, which is what turns two arguments into one film. The single most beautiful pair of frames the place produces — the plan read from above with the camera continuing up through the storeys that are not there, and the curve read from below with the camera continuing up past the spire into sky — is also the clearest statement of the concept, and the second of the two needs no aircraft, which matters because drone permission here should be assumed refused.

And it is kept apart from the other films in this group that share its concepts or its district: the sacred hill east of the city with its riddle put to a king about a mango tree, and the pair of colossal standing figures on the plain to the south-west. This one is flat ground, hard geometry and two masses, one of which has lost its whole and one of which has lost its size. No climb, no riddle, no rock-cut figure, no water and no reflection belongs in it.

historical_thread.story:
The two monuments stand about nine hundred metres apart in a straight line, the colonnade in the oldest monastic precinct of the city and the stupa to the north-east of it, and between them is roughly a kilometre of the ancient capital's ordinary ground.

The Mahavamsa devotes chapter XXVII, 'The Consecrating of the Lohapasada', to the first. It says the pasada was four-sided, a hundred cubits on each side and a hundred cubits in height; that there were nine storeys, with a hundred window-chambers in each storey and a thousand well-arranged chambers in the whole; and that it was covered over with plates of copper, 'and thence came its name, Brazen Palace'. The chronicle credits the work to Dutugemunu (Dutthagamani), who reigned in the second century BCE, says it was built after a drawing of a palace the monks had seen in a heaven, and records that at each of the four gates the king had eight hundred thousand gold pieces laid down, with bundles of garments and pitchers of sugar, oil and honey, proclaiming that no work was to be done there without reward. A first chapter house on the spot is attributed to Devanampiya Tissa a century earlier. The building's later history is a sequence of losses and rebuilds: it burnt in the reign of Saddhatissa and was re-erected at seven storeys; it was repaired under Bhatikabhaya and Amandagamani Abhaya; it was reduced to five storeys under Sirinaga I; it was repaired under Gothabaya and Jetthatissa I; it was destroyed under Mahasena and rebuilt under his successor Sirimeghavanna; it was worked on by Dhatusena, Aggabodhi I, Aggabodhi IV and Manavamma; it was partly destroyed in the Pandyan invasion in the reign of Sena I and rebuilt under Sena II; it was repaired under Kassapa V and Mahinda IV; and it was destroyed again in the Chola invasion at the end of the Anuradhapura period. What stands now is a ground-floor colonnade: about sixteen hundred granite pillars in forty rows of forty, most rising about twelve feet clear of the ground, on a low terrace between the Ruwanwelisaya stupa and the Sri Maha Bodhi. Which building those pillars belong to is not settled. Popular Sri Lankan site pages attribute them to a twelfth-century rebuilding under Parakramabahu I; the English Wikipedia article instead associates the sixteen hundred pillars with Dutugemunu's building, without a citation; no scholarly or excavation source settling the question was found. A small modern chapter house stands on the pillars at the centre and serves as the uposatha venue for the monks of the Mahavihara. Constance Frederica Gordon-Cumming painted the field on 16 June 1873 and wrote her own note on the sheet: 'Brazen Palace. Anarajahpoora. 1600 monoliths. 12 feet above ground. lines of 40 each way — covering a space of 231 feet square', with further notes identifying the gateway to the Bo tree, traders selling to pilgrims and a pilgrims' camp of talipot palm leaves.

The second monument is attributed by the chronicles to King Mahasena, whose reign is usually placed at about 273 to 301 CE, and the work is generally said to have been completed around 301 CE, some accounts crediting the completion to his son Kithsirimevan (Sirimeghavanna). A fragmentary slab inscription of Mahasena was found in the monastery precinct in 1893. The figure repeated across modern sources is an estimated 93.3 million baked bricks, and the stupa is described as the largest brick structure by volume ever built, commonly given as on the order of 233,000 cubic metres, standing on a square platform about 176 metres on a side. The foundation was taken down about 8.5 metres to bedrock; the Mahavamsa's account of preparing such foundations describes elephants with their feet bound in leather treading stones down into the ground, and modern writers note the flooding of excavated ground to watch how it drank as a rough soil test. The materials were specified rather than improvised: bricks of roughly 60 per cent fine sand and 35 per cent clay, with measured load-bearing capacity around 44 kg per square centimetre, laid in a mortar of finely crushed dolomite, limestone, sieved sand and clay, the whole once coated in a lime plaster that is long gone. Completed at about 122 metres, 400 feet, it was reckoned the third-tallest structure on earth, behind only the great pyramids of Khufu and Khafre at Giza. It was rebuilt at reduced height under Parakramabahu I in the twelfth century, the reign to which popular sources also attribute the pillars now standing at the other monument. A British restoration of its square chamber and spire in 1885 failed within a decade and the western section collapsed by 1895; by 1909 the monument stood in jungle. Excavation under the Central Cultural Fund from 1981 found, unexpectedly, that the dome had been raised before the basal terraces, the reverse of the sequence at the other great stupas, and conservation has since proceeded on Siran Deraniyagala's stated policy of minimum additions, using over 1.5 million bricks fired to specification in a kiln built for the purpose. It stands today at roughly 71 metres, bare brick, on a living terrace, with pilgrims on it daily.

The two histories cross at two points, recorded here as layers and used in neither case in the voice. Mahasena, to whom the stupa is credited, is the reign under which the first building is recorded as having been destroyed; and Parakramabahu I, under whom the stupa was rebuilt smaller, is the king to whom popular sources, though not any scholarly source found here, attribute the pillars that now carry the first name.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The old books' first listed kind of concept is the collective concept, defined as what the mind takes to be there because a number of separate materials have been gathered and connected to one another in some particular way — a table, a chair, a bed, a chariot — and illustrated in the other source with the earth, mountains, rivers and the sea. One name laid over a collection of that kind can come apart from its object in exactly two ways, and this pair of monuments supplies one each, close enough to be walked between.

At the colonnade the connecting is gone and the materials are still standing. Every part of the ground floor is present, in order, in a grid a person can walk and count, and the thing the name refers to — a nine-storey building with a copper roof — is entirely absent and has been for most of a millennium. That is the sources' division test with the division already performed: divide a thing and see what survives, because there is no cloth anywhere among the threads. What survived here is the threads, and what did not survive is still what everybody means when they use the name. The history may detach the name a second time: the building was rebuilt again and again, and the stones that carry the name may belong to one of the rebuildings rather than to the building the chronicle describes. The sources do not agree which, and the film says only that.

At the stupa the object is present and it is the magnitude that failed. A single name covers an assemblage of about ninety-three million objects, not one of which is the thing the name refers to, every one of which a person could pick up in one hand; and the thing they were piled into has lost roughly half its height — collapse, a smaller mediaeval rebuild, jungle, then four decades of putting brick back — without the name altering by a letter. A name is what makes a thing known and is not the thing, and here that is a matter of record rather than of argument.

Set in sequence, the two say more than either does alone. The name did not track completeness and it did not track extent. It was never holding the whole and it was never holding the size. That is why the walk between them is the film's argument and not merely its transition. C077 supplies the plainest word for what a name of this kind is doing — khandha, a heap: everything of one kind gathered by the mind into one and called by a single word, characterised also as a portion — and both halves land twice. A complete ground-floor colonnade is a heap and a portion, by the chronicle's count the bottom ninth of something that no longer exists. A stack of newly fired replacement brick sitting in the shade beside the largest brick structure ever built is the same word at two scales in one frame.
what_is_certain: Both monuments exist, are components of the Sacred City of Anuradhapura UNESCO World Heritage property, and are active places of worship inside living monastic precincts.

The colonnade is one of the eight sacred places of the city and stands between the Ruwanwelisaya stupa and the Sri Maha Bodhi inside the Mahavihara precinct; the stupa stands to the north-east, in the Jetavana monastery precinct. The straight-line distance between the two published coordinates used in this record is about nine hundred metres.

What stands today at the first monument is a ground-floor colonnade of stone pillars on a low terrace, laid out as a square grid, conventionally described as forty rows of forty and about sixteen hundred pillars in all, with most of them rising about twelve feet clear of the ground.

The twelve-foot height and the count of sixteen hundred in lines of forty are recorded independently in 1873, in Constance Gordon-Cumming's own pencilled note on her watercolour of the site, dated 16 June that year, and in modern Sri Lankan site descriptions. The same note adds a figure for the extent of the field, read from the Commons image as 231 feet square.

The Mahavamsa, in the chapter titled 'The Consecrating of the Lohapasada', describes a four-sided building a hundred cubits on each side and a hundred cubits high, nine storeys, a hundred window-chambers in each storey, a thousand chambers in all, and a covering of copper plates from which the name comes.
The chronicle attributes that building to Dutugemunu in the second century BCE and a predecessor chapter house on the same spot to Devanampiya Tissa.

The first building was destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly over more than a thousand years, by fire, by deliberate demolition and in invasions, and the sequence of kings who rebuilt or reduced it is set out consistently across the Sri Lankan sources listed below.
A modern chapter house stands on the old pillars at the centre of the grid and is in use as the uposatha venue for the monks of the Mahavihara.
The second monument is built of baked brick and is the largest brick structure by volume ever built.
It stands today at roughly 71 metres and is bare unplastered brick, its lime plaster long lost.
A fragmentary slab inscription of King Mahasena was recovered from the Jetavana monastery premises in 1893, and a mediaeval pillar inscription found at the western frontispiece names the monument.

The stupa's foundation was carried down to bedrock, and its brick and mortar were made to a specification rather than gathered at random: crushed dolomite, limestone, sieved sand and clay in the mortar, and bricks whose measured compressive performance is high by modern standards.
A British restoration of the stupa's upper works in 1885 failed, the western section collapsed by 1895, and the monument was in jungle by 1909.
Conservation of the stupa under the Central Cultural Fund has run since 1981, on a stated policy of minimum additions, with replacement brick fired to specification in a kiln built for the project.

Sri Lankan law requires Department of Archaeology permission for filming at an archaeological site, and drone flight additionally requires Civil Aviation Authority registration and permit; a man was arrested on 17 September 2025 for flying a drone near the Ruwanwelisaya stupa, a few hundred metres from the colonnade, without Department of Archaeology permission.
what_is_disputed: The storey count of the first building is the chronicle's, not a measurement. Nine storeys is what the Mahavamsa says of Dutugemunu's building; the same chronicle tradition then has it rebuilt at seven storeys after the fire, reduced to five under Sirinaga I and raised again to seven. No standing evidence of any upper floor survives, so 'nine storeys' describes a specific building at a specific moment and not the site.

The height and the footprint of the first building do not agree between sources, and there are now three incompatible figures. The chronicle gives a hundred cubits on each side and a hundred cubits high, usually rendered as about 150 feet or 46 metres. Several modern sources, including the English Wikipedia article, state instead that one side measured 400 feet or 120 metres, which contradicts the chronicle outright; no source consulted explains the discrepancy or says what the 400-foot figure measures. Gordon-Cumming's 1873 note gives the standing field as covering a space read as 231 feet square, which agrees with neither. No modern measured extent of the surviving pillar field was found in the sources consulted, and the 1873 figure is an artist's pencilled note, not a survey.

The room and window figures for the first building are commonly garbled. The Mahavamsa says a hundred window-chambers in each storey and a thousand chambers in the building as a whole; a great many modern retellings say a thousand rooms and a hundred windows on each of the nine levels, which is a different and much larger claim. The film uses the chronicle's wording.

The roof material is given as plates of copper in the standard English translation of the chronicle and as bronze tiles in most modern descriptions. Either way the name means the metal roof, and the roof itself is long gone.

Whether the pillars now standing were re-erected in modern times, and whether their present arrangement, spacing and heights are original, could not be established. One Sri Lankan source describes them as 'systematically fixed to the ground', which may or may not describe modern intervention, and the 1873 watercolour shows them already standing in lines. No excavation or conservation report settling the question was found. This record states the uncertainty rather than resolving it, and the film must not assert that the grid as seen is the twelfth-century layout untouched.
The attribution of the first building to Dutugemunu rests on the chronicle. No inscription independently confirming the builder was found in the sources consulted.

The chronicle says the king had gold, cloth and provisions laid at the four gates and proclaimed that no work was to be done there without reward. That is the chronicle's statement about how the work was paid for, made by a tradition with an interest in the king; it is recorded here as what the record says, not as an established fact about the workforce and not as a virtue. Nothing else about how that labour was raised is established in the sources consulted.

The brick count of the stupa is an estimate, not a survey. The figure 93.3 million is repeated almost universally in modern sources, but the derivation is rarely given and no source consulted traces it to a measured count; it should always be spoken as an estimate.

The stupa's original height is also an estimate and the figures differ. About 122 metres, 400 feet, is the usual modern statement; 'a little over 120 metres' is common; at least one scholarly figure caption gives 160 metres. Part of the divergence is that what is being measured — the fourth-century structure or the reduced twelfth-century rebuild — is not always stated. The claim that it was the third-tallest structure on earth on completion follows from the 122-metre figure and inherits its uncertainty.

The volume figure is unstable across sources. The number 233,000 appears in some places as cubic metres of brickwork and in others as square metres of base area, and it cannot be both: a platform 176 metres square is about 31,000 square metres. An 1870 estimate by L. Liesching put the brickwork at 456,071 cubic yards, roughly 349,000 cubic metres, which is half as much again as the 233,000 figure.
Mahasena's reign dates are given variously as about 273-301 CE and about 276-303 CE, and the completion of the stupa is credited in some accounts to Mahasena and in others to his son Kithsirimevan.

How the stupa's workforce was raised is not established. The record consulted is effectively silent on it for this monument. The well-known chronicle passage about a king refusing unpaid labour and paying every workman belongs to a different and earlier stupa in the same city and cannot be transferred to it; the film states nothing about who built it beyond what is recorded, and narrates none of it as devotion, sacrifice or glory.

The destructions and the quarrel are recorded by parties to them. The chronicle tradition that records the demolition of the first building under Mahasena, and the damage to it in the Pandyan and Chola invasions, was written and continued by the community whose building it was; the same tradition holds that Mahasena, under the influence of the monk Sanghamitta, acted against that older community and that the second monastery was founded on ground connected with them. The film records the episodes as layers of the sites' history with their provenance attached, does not adjudicate any of them, and narrates none of them as anyone's grievance or anyone's due.

The stupa's own identification was wrong for a long time, and the two great stupas' names were in effect swapped. Sri Lankan site histories (Amazing Lanka, Lanka Pradeepa) say the British identified this stupa as Abhayagiri in 1873-74, and the English Wikipedia article on Abhayagiri Vihara says the Abhayagiri ruins were 'mistakenly identified at first as Jetavana Vihara' when they were photographed and drawn in the late nineteenth century; the same site histories say the matter was settled by a pillar inscription of about the eighth to tenth century found at the western frontispiece, naming the monument Dena Vehera. The swap is confirmed by those two independent kinds of source; the 1873-74 date and the inscription's role rest on the Sri Lankan site pages and were not checked against a survey report or an epigraphic publication. This is recorded as a layer of the site's history; the film does not build on it and nothing of it enters the voice, because a disputed identification is another film's subject in this group.

Recent cement additions to the stupa's outer layers, made in good faith, are now thought by archaeologists to have accelerated deterioration rather than prevented it — a live conservation disagreement rather than a settled fact.

Reign dates for several of the kings in the first building's sequence differ by a few years between sources, and the same king's name appears in more than one spelling. The record uses the forms in the Sri Lankan sources listed and treats all the dates as approximate.

Which building the standing pillars belong to, and who raised them. Popular Sri Lankan site pages and travel articles (for example Lanka Pradeepa and Amusing Planet) attribute them to a twelfth-century rebuilding under Parakramabahu I; the English Wikipedia article instead associates the sixteen hundred pillars with Dutugemunu's building, without a citation; no scholarly publication, inscription or excavation report settling the question was found, and a chronicle passage tying these particular stones to either king was not located. An earlier version of this record called the Parakramabahu attribution unanimous; it is not, and it is not used in the voice. That Parakramabahu I is also credited with rebuilding the stupa smaller is recorded as a layer, and nothing is inferred from the coincidence.

what_to_film: One avenue of the pillar field at first light, camera low and square on, forty stones receding in a single line, before the through-traffic between the two great monuments builds up.
A slow lateral walk across the face of the field, long enough that the rows come into alignment, collapse and realign several times. This is the shot that makes the grid an event rather than a fact.
A single pillar at arm's length: lichen, tool marks, the seating notch near the top, the broken crown. Then a pull back that puts it among hundreds without a cut.

The modern chapter house in the middle, standing on the old pillars at first-floor height, with a long tilt up past its roofline into empty sky. This is the ground version of the first vertical and it must be shot whether or not the drone flies.

The first vertical in its best form, if permission is granted: a straight lift from between two pillars, rising until forty rows of forty resolve into one ruled rectangle, and continuing up through the levels that are not there. No horizontal drone move is needed and none should be attempted over the precinct.

The honest fallback for the same frame if the drone is refused: a raised position outside the precinct for the plan at an angle, a long lens compressing the rows into a solid wall of stone, and the held tilt into empty sky, which carries the argument on its own.

The traverse itself, as one continuous move or as a small number of long takes on the public route: out through the gate, down the steps, along the path, past low foundations and stone posts, with the dome coming up over the canopy ahead and growing. This is the spine of the film and it is filmed as a walk, not as a montage of what is passed.
Arrival at the stupa: sandals in rows at the edge of the paving, bare feet on hot stone, and the moment at the base where the curve stops fitting in the frame.

One of the four projecting frontispieces, static and square on and then steeply from below, with dressed stone set into brick courses and the dome's brickwork running away above it — the shot where the scale gap is unarguable.

The payoff: from the paving at the base, a single unbroken tilt straight up the flank through the courses, the shoulder of the dome, the square chamber, the spire and the scaffold, into sky, held as long as the first vertical was held. Long lens where the geometry needs compressing. No aircraft required.

The conservation work, with consent: replacement brick stacked in heaps in the shade, lime mortar being turned, and two hands setting one brick into a patched section of the skin. Real work, happening anyway, nothing laid to order.

The shadow field at the colonnade at each end of the day, as texture and as a clock: the shadows of sixteen hundred uprights ruling the earth and swinging round. Not as a revelation of the plan, which belongs to another film, and not as the payoff.

The closing frame at distance and without intrusion, from ground that holds both monuments in one sightline if such ground exists: the field of uprights flat and dark, the dome behind it, lamps lit at each, nobody approached and nothing lit by the crew.

Ambient sound to picture: bare feet on hot earth and on stone, the specific dead acoustic of standing among hundreds of stone uprights in the open, the change in that acoustic on the walk, a trowel, crows, wind across an open plain, and the through-traffic of a working precinct.
suggested_location.access: Both monuments are inside the Anuradhapura sacred city, part of the Sacred City of Anuradhapura UNESCO World Heritage property, reached by road from Anuradhapura new town and normally visited on foot. The colonnade is one of the eight sacred places of the city and stands on the circuit between the Ruwanwelisaya stupa and the Sri Maha Bodhi; the stupa is about nine hundred metres to the north-east inside the Jetavana monastery precinct, and the walk between the two is on ordinary public routes through the old city. Ticketing for the sacred city and whether the Cultural Triangle ticket still covers each precinct have changed more than once and should be checked. Both are active places of worship: shoes and headwear come off, dress is covered, and white or light clothing is the norm. The pillar field stands on a low terrace enclosed by an iron railing, entered by a gate and a short flight of steps on the axis that leads through the pillars to the modern chapter house in the centre, which is in use by the resident community and is not a visitor attraction. The stupa's terrace is busy from before dawn. Filming at an archaeological site requires Department of Archaeology permission, and the agreement of the monastic custodians is a separate matter from the Department's — and these are two separate communities, so it is two separate agreements, not one. Drone flight needs Civil Aviation Authority registration and permit plus Department of Archaeology clearance; unauthorised flying at this city's monuments has led to arrests, including one reported on 17 September 2025 a few hundred metres from the colonnade, and permission should be assumed refused until it is granted in writing.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry months of roughly May to September for hard light and open sky. This film wants the middle of the day more than most: the shadows shorten to nothing, the pillar field reads purely as a plan, and the brick mass reads as course and volume rather than as a silhouette. The first hour gives the avenues and the walk, and a morning traverse keeps the sun behind or beside the camera on the north-easterly leg between the two. After the north-east rains, roughly December to February, the earth is dark, the lichen is bright, the brick is deeper and the light is softer, which is a different and equally good film. Full-moon days fill both precincts and are the hardest days on which to film anyone respectfully; they should be a deliberate choice and not a default. The last twenty minutes of sun on the brick curve are beautiful and are deliberately not this film's payoff.

suggested_location.research_note:
This record is a merge of two previously separate location records and all of the research in it is desk research from published sources, none of it checked on the ground. For the colonnade: the chronicle description — nine storeys, a hundred cubits square and a hundred cubits high, a hundred window-chambers to each storey, a thousand chambers in all, copper plates on the roof, the drawing brought from a heaven, and the gold laid at the four gates — is quoted from the standard English translation of Mahavamsa chapter XXVII as published at the two chronicle sites listed. The sequence of destructions and rebuilds, the number and arrangement of the pillars, their twelve-foot height above ground, the popular attribution of the standing pillars to the twelfth-century structure of Parakramabahu I (now held in what_is_disputed; see below) and the identification of the small central building as the modern uposathaghara of the Mahavihara are from the Sri Lankan site record listed. For the stupa: builder, dates, brick count, heights, base dimensions, foundation depth, brick and mortar composition, the 1885 British restoration and its failure, the jungle condition by 1909, the 1981 start of Central Cultural Fund conservation, the minimum-additions policy, the dome-before-terraces excavation finding and the nineteenth-century misidentification are all from the sources listed and were carried over from the record being absorbed, where they had been verified in the same way.

`coordinates` is the point given for the colonnade in the encyclopedia entry; `secondary_coordinates` is the Wikidata point for the stupa, which agrees with the geotag on one of the Commons photographs used here. The distance of about nine hundred metres between them is computed from those two published points and is a straight line, not a walking distance; the walk is longer and has not been measured or walked. The elevation figure is the approximate elevation of the city and not a surveyed figure for either terrace.

Every quantitative figure for the stupa is an estimate and the significant disagreements between sources are set out in what_is_disputed rather than averaged away, including the unstable 233,000 figure. For the colonnade, the commonly repeated modern figure of 400 feet to a side contradicts the chronicle's hundred cubits and is carried into what_is_disputed rather than reconciled; a third figure has now been added to that entry, because the pencilled note on the 1873 watercolour gives the field as covering a space read as 231 feet square. That figure was read off the Commons image of the watercolour at 1400 pixels wide during this rewrite and has not been checked against a catalogue transcription, so it is recorded as a reading of an artist's note and not as a measurement. Two things remain searched for and not found: any modern measured extent of the surviving pillar field, and any excavation or conservation report establishing whether the pillars were re-erected in modern times or whether their present arrangement, spacing and heights are original. One AI-generated encyclopedia page offering a measured grid dimension and pillar cross-sections was found in the earlier round of research and was deliberately not used or cited.

Current ticketing, Department of Archaeology filming permission, both resident communities' positions, the current state and position of conservation scaffolding, and drone permission are all unverified; drone permission in particular should be assumed refused. Thirteen images are carried here: the six found for the colonnade and the five found for the stupa in the two earlier rounds, all of which were found through the Commons search API and looked at before their captions were first written, and two added in this rewrite for the from-below geometry the merged treatment needs, both found through the search API and looked at before captioning. All thirteen were re-confirmed to exist through the titles API on 25 September 2026 before being written into this file, and the watercolour was re-examined at higher resolution so that its pencilled note could be quoted. Independent corroboration of the drone incident near the great stupa was found after these records were written: a press report (Daily FT, 'Drone camera hits pinnacle of Ruwanweli Maha Seya in Anuradhapura') states that a camera drone being flown for an unpermitted shoot struck the pinnacle of the stupa, that police reported no damage to the stupa or its pinnacle, and that the operator was arrested and his equipment seized under the Archaeological Sites of National Importance Act and was to be produced before the Anuradhapura Magistrate's Court. That report does not carry the date, so the specific date of 17 September 2025 still rests on the police notice alone. The substance — an arrest and a seizure under that Act for flying here without permission — is corroborated, and the detail that the aircraft hit the monument is the strongest argument for the ground fallback this film already carries.

Corrections of 26 September 2026 (GRP-01 audit). The attribution of the standing pillars to Parakramabahu I's twelfth-century rebuild is carried only by popular pages; the English Wikipedia article associates the pillars with Dutugemunu's building instead, uncited, and no scholarly source was found either way. It was removed from the voice (beat 3 now says only that the sources do not agree which rebuilding the pillars belong to, or whose it was), the 'unanimous' line was deleted from what_is_certain, the matter was moved to what_is_disputed, and the drop_if that depended on it was removed because the film no longer does. The voice also no longer names Parakramabahu or Mahasena, who are named in other films' voices in this group, and it no longer picks between the accounts that credit the stupa's completion to Mahasena and to his son Kithsirimevan. 'The bottom fortieth' was an arithmetic slip for a nine-storey building and now reads 'by the chronicle's count the bottom ninth', and beat 4 now attributes the nine storeys to the chronicle, whose tradition also gives seven and five. The Jetavana/Abhayagiri naming swap was re-verified on 26 September against the English Wikipedia article on Abhayagiri Vihara and kept in what_is_disputed; its 1873-74 date rests on the Sri Lankan site histories. District: Anuradhapura District stands at nine films in the slate's Films per district table, above the seven at which a district is treated as closed, and GRP-01 puts IDEA-0002, IDEA-0008 and IDEA-0012 there. The film holds because both of its monuments, and the merge that joined them, are in this city and nowhere else; the cost is stated here and in risks, not hidden.

unknowns: No access, permission or contact has been sought or confirmed at either monument. Everything here is a research direction.

Whether the Department of Archaeology will permit filming at the two monuments, and on what conditions, is unverified; the agreement of each resident monastic community is a separate question, and they are two different communities, so there are at least three permissions to obtain and none has been sought.
Whether the walk between the two can be filmed as a continuous journey on the public route, and whether a camera moving along it can avoid making anyone identifiable on a busy day, is unassessed.

Drone permission over this precinct is genuinely doubtful and may simply be refused. Civil Aviation Authority registration and permit plus Department of Archaeology clearance are both required, and a man was arrested in September 2025 for flying a drone at the great stupa a few hundred metres from the colonnade without archaeological permission. Because the overhead rectangle is the best version of the first vertical, the film is written so that it survives refusal: beat 4 makes the vertical argument from the ground with a held tilt from the chapter house roofline into empty sky, the grid is legible along the avenues at eye level, a raised position outside the precinct gives the plan at an angle, and the payoff at the second monument is a tilt from the paving that needs no aircraft.

Whether the pillars were re-erected in modern times, and whether their present arrangement, spacing and heights are original, could not be established from the sources consulted. This needs an excavation or conservation report or a Department of Archaeology answer before anything about the grid's authenticity is said on screen.

No modern measured extent of the surviving pillar field was found; the only figures available are the chronicle's, the contradictory modern 400-foot figure, and the reading of an artist's 1873 pencilled note.
The brick count, the original height and the volume of the stupa are estimates that differ between sources; no source consulted gives a derivation for the 93.3 million figure.

Whether conservation work will be active, and accessible to a camera with consent, during any given filming window is unknown, and one shot in what_to_film depends on it; the scaffolding position also changes from year to year.

How close a camera may work inside the railing at the colonnade, and whether the central chapter house may be filmed from outside at all, is unknown; the formal monastic proceedings held there are not a public event and the film assumes they are closed.
Whether any ground exists from which both monuments can be held in one sightline for the closing frame has not been established, and the closing beat is written so that it works without it.
Whether a full-moon day is filmable at all without intruding on people who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera has not been assessed on the ground at either site.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal, and a merge of two earlier location proposals. The locations were proposed by Claude and confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25; that verdict was reset to pending on 2026-09-26 after an audit corrected voice lines, and the film is again awaiting his review. Their supporting detail is desk research from published sources and is unverified. The chronicle's figures are the chronicle's, not measurements, and every quantitative figure for the second monument is an estimate. No scene or shot is decided here.
